clue.text: Novel few liked about a cathedral city

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go round the A
novel means new or unusual, so these letters are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A reader complains that hardly anyone enjoyed a book set in a cathedral town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a noun (and The Vicar of Wakefield is one), but it is the anagram signal: FEW LIKED is rearranged and placed 'about' A.
explanation.definitionFit: Wakefield in West Yorkshire has an Anglican cathedral and city status, so it is an example of a cathedral city.

clue.text: What's raised to get a good present?

definitions.text: What's raised to get a good present?

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: taken as written
the present moment is now

explanation.surface: A question about how to scrape together the means for a nice gift.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'raised' reverses A G NOW. WONGA is British slang for money, which is what gets raised to buy a good present.
explanation.definitionFit: Cash is what fundraisers raise and what buys a gift; this slang word for money fits the whole clue.

clue.text: Make progress as Australian skipper

parts.note: a skipper is anything that hops, and Australia's famous hopper is the marsupial; the phrase also names a learner driver's jerky stop-start progress

explanation.surface: Advice on how to advance like an Australian captain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skipper' reads as a team captain, but here it is a jumping animal. The phrase is also British slang for a car lurching forward when a learner mishandles the clutch.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving forward the way a bounding marsupial does is literally hopping, which the idiom describes.

clue.text: Strawberries grow in fringes of fields

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other
the fringes of a word are its outermost letters, first and last

parts.note: to grow crops is to raise them

explanation.surface: Strawberries are cultivated around the edges of farmland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fringes of' takes F and S from 'fields', and RAISE goes 'in' between them.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the French word for the soft red fruit, sometimes used on English menus.

clue.text: Models' fee is different, without clothes

definitions.note: plural noun; the apostrophe is the surface's possessive

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the shuffled letters surround the next piece
different signals that the letters appear in another order

parts.note: fig means dress or attire, as in 'in full fig'

explanation.surface: A modelling agency's fee changes when the models pose nude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without clothes' suggests nudity, but 'without' means outside: an anagram of FEE IS (EFIES) goes around FIG, the old word for dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Effigies are sculpted or modelled likenesses of people, so models in that sense.

clue.text: One egg in twelve for German head of state

indicators.note: in places the egg inside the abbreviation for twelve

parts.note: doz is the abbreviation for dozen, which is twelve
a nit is a single egg of a louse

explanation.surface: A cook takes one egg out of a box of twelve for a German leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One egg' tempts I plus O, but it is a single louse egg; 'in' puts it inside the dozen abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Admiral Karl Dönitz briefly succeeded Hitler as Germany's leader in May 1945.

clue.text: Artist's taken back verse replacing new words

indicators.note: replacing means one letter is swapped in for another
taken back means the painter's surname is read in reverse

parts.note: Francis Bacon was a famous British painter

explanation.surface: A painter withdraws some lines of poetry and substitutes fresh vocabulary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken back' turns BACON into NOCAB; then 'verse replacing new' swaps its N for V.
explanation.definitionFit: Vocab is a short informal form of vocabulary, the stock of words someone knows.

clue.text: Expressing change of heart, then clearing out

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, and here that letter is changed for another

parts.note: voicing an opinion is expressing it

explanation.surface: Someone says they have changed their mind and then empties a room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change of heart' alters only the middle letter of VOICING, C becoming D.
explanation.definitionFit: To void something is to empty or evacuate it, so voiding is emptying out.

clue.text: Goodness?. Chef's squeezed out the last bit

indicators.note: squeezing out the last bit drops the final letter of the word

parts.note: a chef is a cook; the 's stands for 'has'

explanation.surface: An exclamation as a chef presses out the final drop of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Coo is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'goodness!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild interjections expressing surprise or astonishment.

clue.text: May imb floppy in case tuck into this?

indicators.note: in puts the shuffled letters inside the container

parts.note: a box is a case or container

indicators.note: floppy suggests something loose and shapeless, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clumsy instruction to place something loose in a box for eating.
explanation.walkthrough: The page's 'gmb' is an OCR slip for 'imb'; only then does 'floppy' give the six letters that go 'in' the case.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck is British slang for snack food, and this spicy Indian snack mixture is something one tucks into.

clue.text: Jack stops girl becoming Eastern agent

indicators.note: stops in the sense of plugging a gap, so the card letter sits inside the name

parts.note: Nina is a girl's name
J is the abbreviation for jack in cards

explanation.surface: A man halts a young woman as she turns into a spy from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stops' means fills a hole, so J goes inside NINA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninjas were Japanese covert operatives trained in espionage and assassination.

clue.text: Like simple life as conscript, getting into sport and fitness

indicators.note: getting into means entering, so the soldier goes inside the other letters

parts.note: sport in the sense of fun or amusement
form means fitness, as an athlete's condition
GI is an American enlisted soldier

explanation.surface: A recruit takes up games and exercise to enjoy a basic existence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'simple life' is not a carefree lifestyle but a lowly organism, fungi; GI goes 'into' FUN + FORM.
explanation.definitionFit: Fungiform means shaped like a mushroom, so resembling a basic organism such as a fungus.

clue.text: Book's foreign edition brought in an old man's tale

indicators.note: brought in means placed inside the other pieces

parts.note: an gives the indefinite article A
the old man is Pa, father, here with possessive s
a saga is a long story or tale

indicators.note: foreign means strange or alien, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An overseas printing of a book is introduced into an elderly man's story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book's' looks possessive, but the 's is just 'is'. 'foreign' rearranges the edition letters to ETOINDI, and 'brought in' sets them inside the old man's tale, just before its final A.
explanation.definitionFit: E M Forster's 1924 novel about British India is a celebrated literary work.

clue.text: They maintain food is still found under the sea

indicators.note: in a down clue the second piece goes beneath the first

parts.note: the deep is a poetic name for the sea
freezes means stops moving, keeps still

explanation.surface: Something said to preserve food is discovered on the ocean floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found under' places FREEZES below DEEP in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Freezers preserve food for long periods, keeping it from spoiling.

clue.text: Future, initially brighter without wife, cared for less

indicators.note: initially picks out the opening letter of the word
without in its old sense of outside, so the comparative goes round the abbreviation

parts.note: rosier means brighter or more hopeful

explanation.surface: A man's prospects were sunnier without his spouse, though he was less looked after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without wife' seems to drop a W, but 'without' means outside: ROSIER wraps W, after F.
explanation.definitionFit: Frowsy means scruffy and unkempt, so frowsier describes something more neglected.

clue.text: Perhaps unfairly give bird front beak?

parts.note: fore means front, as in the forepart of a ship
beak is British slang for a magistrate or judge

explanation.surface: Is it unfair to give a bird a prominent bill?
explanation.walkthrough: 'bird' is British slang for a prison sentence (birdtime), and 'beak' is slang for a magistrate.
explanation.definitionFit: To forejudge is to decide a case before hearing it, which may hand down a jail term unjustly.

clue.text: Bright start's left a couple under par in the morning

indicators.note: the start has left, so the first letter is removed

parts.note: an eagle in golf is a score two strokes below par
AM, ante meridiem, means in the morning

explanation.surface: A golfer's sparkling opening: two under par before noon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start's left' reads as 'the start has left', dropping the first letter to leave AGLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Agleam means shining or gleaming, so brightly lit.

clue.text: Sea bird spotted having made Channel

parts.note: a gull is a common seabird
eyed means looked at, spotted

explanation.surface: A seagull was seen after crossing the English Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' looks like the English Channel but is a ditch: gulley as a verb means to cut a channel.
explanation.definitionFit: A gulley is a water channel, so to gulley is to form one; past tense means having cut it.

clue.text: Make employee over in Ireland hot after runs

indicators.note: after means the following piece comes later than the abbreviation for runs

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation inside the country's name

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Taking on a worker again in sweltering Ireland after he flees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' means again here, part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehire is to take someone on again as staff, making them an employee once more.

clue.text: Item of litter around port makes one go crazy

indicators.note: around means the first piece surrounds the second

parts.note: a runt is the smallest animal in a litter
Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port

explanation.surface: A piece of rubbish blown about a harbour drives someone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'litter' is not rubbish but a brood of young animals.
explanation.definitionFit: To run riot is an idiom for behaving wildly and without restraint.

clue.text: Spot on sensitive skin: no lasting cure

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means the second piece follows the first

parts.note: the quick is the tender flesh under a fingernail
a spot, a tight situation, is a fix

explanation.surface: A pimple on delicate skin has no permanent remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' looks like a blemish but means a predicament.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick fix is an expedient solution that does not resolve the underlying problem.

clue.text: After century, round about five I like a bowl

indicators.note: after means the century abbreviation comes first in the answer, the rest following

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for century, a hundred

indicators.note: round means the number word surrounds the other letters

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
ca, circa, means about
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: A batsman scores a hundred and then wants to bowl his five-over spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'century' and 'bowl' suggest cricket, but 'bowl' belongs to the definition; 'round' wraps the number word around the other letters, and 'After' puts them behind C.
explanation.definitionFit: Concave means curving inwards, hollow as the inside of a dish.

clue.text: Agent upping power with revolutionary spirit

indicators.note: in a down clue, upping lifts a letter higher, nearer the top

parts.note: a spy is a secret agent
Che Guevara was the Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: A spy gains power with the aid of a revolutionary's fervour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upping power' moves P to the top of SPY, giving PSY.
explanation.definitionFit: The psyche is the human soul or mind, the animating spirit.

clue.text: Light planes near a jet flying north

indicators.note: flying suggests things scattered through the air, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Aircraft approach a jet heading northwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' seems an aircraft adjective but is the definition, a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A Japanese lantern is a paper lamp, a decorative source of illumination.

clue.text: Boy or girl can, over year

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: can and nick are both slang for prison

explanation.surface: A child may be put in a tin, and then left there a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' is slang for jail, as is NICK.
explanation.definitionFit: This name is used for males and females alike, short for Nicholas or Nicola.

clue.text: Confessed drug taker you'd recalled eating fruit

indicators.note: eating means taking in, so the reversed letters surround the fruit
recalled means called back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: you'd, in archaic form, is ye'd
a quince is a hard, pear-like fruit

explanation.surface: An addict recalls that you consumed some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns YED (ye'd) into DEY, which 'eating' QUINCE gives DE QUINCE Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas De Quincey wrote Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, admitting his laudanum habit.

clue.text: As square as a Manx cat?

indicators.note: a Manx cat famously has no tail, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a quad is a college square or quadrangle

explanation.surface: Is someone as conventional as a tailless cat?
explanation.walkthrough: Qua is Latin for 'in the capacity of', so 'as'.
explanation.definitionFit: Qua is used in English to mean in the role of, the same as one use of the small conjunction.

clue.text: Old warrior queen's narrated account

indicators.note: narrated means spoken, so the sound of the queen's name gives the letters

parts.note: Queen Anne, with a possessive s

explanation.surface: A former soldier's story about a queen is told.
explanation.walkthrough: 'queen's' spoken sounds like ANZ, then AC.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anzac was a soldier of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps in the First World War.

clue.text: Careless backing into outsider in lift

indicators.note: into places the reversed letters inside the other piece

parts.note: ET, the extraterrestrial, is an outsider from another world

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: lax means careless or slack

explanation.surface: A negligent person reverses into a stranger in an elevator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns LAX into XAL, which goes 'into' ET.
explanation.definitionFit: To exalt is to raise someone in rank or esteem, a figurative elevating.

clue.text: Boy going in goal, not up front all the time

indicators.note: going in means the name is placed inside the other letters

parts.note: an end is a goal or aim
sly means sneaky, not open
Les is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A lad keeps goal but never plays forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goal' and 'up front' suggest football, but 'not up front' means sneaky, and 'going in' sets the name in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Endlessly means without stopping, continually.
